section.title: The Day of the Lord
section.sectionRationale: Peter turns from the false teachers to the doubt they spread: that Christ will never return. He answers the scoffers of the last days by appealing to God's word, which once judged the world by water and now reserves it for fire. The seeming delay is not slowness but patience, for the Lord measures time differently and is not willing that any should perish. When the Day comes it will come like a thief, dissolving the heavens and the elements, and God's people wait for a new heaven and a new earth where righteousness dwells.
section.thesis: The apparent delay of the Day of the Lord is not God's failure to keep His promise but His patience toward sinners; the same word that made and once flooded the world holds it now for fire, so that when the Day comes suddenly and the present order is dissolved, believers who look for the new heaven and new earth should live in holiness and godliness.
section.frameNote: Four movements: the scoffers of the last days, verses 1 to 4; God's word over past and coming judgment, verses 5 to 7; the Lord not slow but patient, verses 8 to 9; and the Day of the Lord and the new creation, verses 10 to 13.

units.label: Scoffers in the last days
units.note: where is the promise of His coming

verses.text: Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking
by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles.
Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days {{empaiktai|scoffers}} will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires.
“Where is the promise of {{parousia|His coming}}?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.”

units.label: The word that judges
units.note: once by water, now reserved for fire

verses.text: But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water,
through which the world of that time perished in the flood.
And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.

units.label: Not slow, but patient
units.note: not willing that any should perish

verses.text: Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like {{chilia|a thousand years}}, and a thousand years are like a day.
The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is {{makrothumei|patient}} with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to {{metanoia|repentance}}.

units.label: The Day and the new creation
units.note: like a thief, then righteousness dwells

verses.text: But the Day of the Lord will come like a {{kleptes|thief}}. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the {{stoicheia|elements}} will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.
Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness
as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat.
But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a {{kainos|new}} heaven and a new earth, where {{dikaiosyne|righteousness}} dwells.

empaiktai.gloss: Mockers, scoffers, those who make sport of what is sacred. In the last days such men will jeer at the promise of Christ's return, and their scoffing is driven not by reason but by their own evil desires. They mock the coming judgment because they do not want it to be true.

parousia.gloss: Presence, arrival, coming, the standard word for the royal visit of a king. Used of the return of Christ in glory, His parousia is the promise the scoffers deny. The whole hope of the church rests on the certainty of His coming.

chilia.gloss: A thousand years. Echoing Psalm 90:4, Peter reminds believers that God is not bound by time as we are: a day and a thousand years are alike to Him. What looks like delay to impatient men is nothing to the eternal God who keeps His own perfect timing.

makrothumei.gloss: To be long-suffering, patient, slow to anger. The seeming delay of the Day is in fact God's patience, holding back judgment to give room for repentance. His slowness, so called, is mercy: He is not willing that any should perish.

metanoia.gloss: A change of mind and heart, repentance, a turning from sin to God. God's patience has a purpose: that sinners come to repentance. The interval before the Day is the space of grace in which the gospel calls men to turn and live.

kleptes.gloss: A thief. The Day of the Lord will come like a thief, unannounced and unexpected, catching the careless unprepared. The image, drawn from Jesus' own teaching, presses the call to watchfulness: no one knows the hour, so all must be ready.

stoicheia.gloss: The elements, the basic constituents of the physical world. On the Day these will be destroyed, or dissolved, by fire. Peter pictures the undoing of the present created order, the whole fabric of the world laid bare before its Maker and Judge.

kainos.gloss: New in kind and quality, not merely new in time. The promised new heaven and new earth are not just a fresh copy of the old but a renewed creation, cleansed and glorious, where righteousness is at home. This is the hope that shapes how believers live now.

dikaiosyne.gloss: Righteousness, conformity to what is right, the settled character of God Himself. In the new creation righteousness dwells, is at home, permanently. The world to come is not merely free of sin but full of the righteousness the scoffers now despise.

basic.context: Peter writes to stir wholesome thinking against a rising doubt. In the last days mockers arise, ruled by their own desires, sneering that Christ has not returned and that life simply goes on as always. Peter answers on three fronts. First, the scoffers wilfully forget history: the same word of God that made the world once destroyed it by the flood, and that word now holds the present world for fire on the day of judgment. Second, the delay is not slowness but patience; God is not bound by time, and He withholds judgment so that sinners may repent. Third, the Day will come suddenly, like a thief, dissolving the heavens and the elements in fire. Because all this is coming, believers should live holy and godly lives, waiting for the new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage is prophetic and eschatological, teaching about the return of Christ and the end of the age. Read it in light of Jesus' own words about His coming as a thief and no one knowing the day or hour. Two matters draw special care. First, the so-called delay of the Day: what looks to the scoffers like a broken promise is, in Peter's answer, the outworking of God's patience. Second, the language of fire, dissolving elements, and the earth laid bare: interpreters differ on whether this describes the annihilation of the present cosmos or its purifying renewal into the new creation of verse 13.
basic.originalLanguages: In the last days come empaiktai, scoffers, who deny the parousia, the coming of Christ. Peter answers that with the Lord a day is like chilia ete, a thousand years; He is not slow but makrothumei, patient, willing all to come to metanoia, repentance. Yet the Day will come like a kleptes, a thief, when the stoicheia, the elements, are dissolved by fire, and believers await a kainos, a qualitatively new, heaven and earth where dikaiosyne, righteousness, dwells.
basic.typology: The flood of Noah's day is a type of the coming judgment: as the ancient world perished by water at God's word, so the present world is reserved for fire by that same word. The pattern of a world judged and a remnant preserved points forward to the final Day and to the new creation that follows, cleansed and secure.
basic.christ: The whole passage hangs on the certainty of Christ's coming. The promise the scoffers deny is the promise of His parousia, His royal return in glory. He is the Lord whose Day this is, the Judge before whom the elements dissolve, and the Savior whose patience now holds open the door of repentance. The new heaven and new earth are His inheritance shared with His people, and it is knowing Him that makes the believer ready for the Day that comes like a thief.
basic.god: God is Creator and Judge, whose word made the heavens and the earth, once destroyed the world by flood, and now keeps it for fire. He is sovereign over time, to whom a thousand years are as a day, so that no promise of His can fail through delay. And He is patient and merciful, not willing that any should perish, holding back the Day so that sinners may repent. His justice and His mercy meet in the interval before the end.
basic.crossReferences: Psalm 90:4 stands behind verse 8, a thousand years as a day in God's sight. Matthew 24:36-44 gives Jesus' teaching on the unknown day and the thief. Genesis 6 to 8 tells of the flood, the pattern of verses 5 to 7. And Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise the new heavens and new earth fulfilled in Revelation 21:1.
basic.oneStory: From creation to flood to the coming fire, God's word governs the whole story of the world, and it moves toward a settled end: a new heaven and new earth where righteousness is at home. The scoffers read history as an endless sameness, but Scripture reads it as a road to the Day of the Lord. Between the promise and its fulfilment stands God's patience, the space of grace in which the gospel of the returning Christ calls sinners to repent before that Day arrives.

context.literary:
The chapter opens by looking back and closes by looking forward, and in between it is built as a debate. Verses 1 and 2 define the letter as a reminder, naming two sources of authority that must stand together: what was foretold by the prophets and what the Lord commanded through the apostles. Verses 3 and 4 give the objection in the scoffers' own words, a quotation in the text. Verses 5 to 7 answer by history, verses 8 and 9 by the character of God, verse 10 by the fact of the Day, and verses 11 to 13 by the life that fits it. Each answer begins with an address, 'Beloved', in verses 1, 8 and 14 and again in 15 and 17, which marks the turning points like beats in a drum.

The sentences in verses 5 to 7 form a close parallel. 'By God's word' the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water; 'by that same word' the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire. The same agent, the word, stands behind creation, the flood and the coming judgment, and the repeated pair of heavens and earth ties the three into one story. Water destroyed the world 'of that time', and fire awaits 'the present' one, so the argument is that the world has changed before, and in the very way the scoffers say cannot be.

The long description of the Day in verses 10 to 12 is an example of repetition used for force. The elements 'destroyed by fire' appear in verse 10, 'destroyed' again in verse 11 and 'melt' in verse 12, so that three times in a few lines the world is described as dissolving. The reader is not allowed to skim past it.

The pivot is verse 11: 'what kind of people ought you to be?' All the cosmic scenery serves a question about character. And the paragraph ends at verse 13 with a positive image, the very opposite of dissolving, a home where righteousness dwells. The passage moves from mockery to a promise, and the line that connects them is the call to holy living.
context.historical:
Peter's scoffers belong to a world with two strong ideas about the end. The Epicureans taught that the gods did not meddle with the world and that there would be no judgment, so the taunt 'everything continues as it has' would have sounded sensible to educated people. The Stoics, by contrast, taught that the cosmos would periodically be consumed by fire and reborn, and the language of a fiery end was therefore not strange in the Greek world. Peter's point is not to borrow either theory but to say that the biblical account of a creating and judging God is the only one that accounts for both the world's origin and its end.

The objection 'Where is the promise?' is old. Jeremiah's hearers said, 'Where is the word of the LORD? Let it come now!', Jeremiah 17:15, Malachi's said, 'Where is the God of justice?', Malachi 2:17, and Ezekiel had to answer a proverb in Israel, 'The days go by, and every vision fails', Ezekiel 12:22. Isaiah 5:19 records mockers who said, 'Let Him hurry and hasten His work.' Peter is not facing a new kind of unbelief. He is facing a perennial one.

The 'fathers' who 'fell asleep' are most naturally the earlier generations of believers. In the New Testament 'the fathers' often means Israel's ancestors, as in Hebrews 1:1, and 'fell asleep' is the regular Christian term for death, as in 1 Corinthians 15:51. By the time of Peter's second letter a generation of Christians, including some of the apostles, was passing away, and the delay of the Lord's return was an obvious problem for the churches. Peter himself expects to die soon, 1:14.

Peter calls this 'my second letter', and speaks of 'your apostles' and of Paul's letters, 3:15 and 16. The first letter is most likely 1 Peter. The mention of 'the last days' fits the early Christian belief that the last days had begun with Christ, as Acts 2:17 and Hebrews 1:2 say, so that Peter's readers were already living in them.
context.canonical:
The chapter draws on three strands of Scripture. The first is creation and the flood. Peter's 'formed out of water and by water' recalls Genesis 1:2 and 1:9, where the dry land appears when God speaks, and psalms that say the LORD founded the earth upon the waters, Psalm 24:2, and made the heavens by His word, Psalm 33:6. The flood of verse 6 returns to Genesis 6 to 8, and Jesus makes the same comparison in Matthew 24:37 to 39.

The second strand is the Day of the LORD in the prophets. Amos 5:18 warns those who long for it that it will be darkness and not light. Joel 2:1 and Zephaniah 1:14 to 18 speak of a day of gloom, and Zephaniah 1:18 and 3:8 say 'the whole earth will be consumed by the fire of His jealousy'. Isaiah 34:4 says the heavens will be dissolved, and Malachi 4:1 pictures a burning furnace. Isaiah 66:15 to 16 says the LORD will come with fire. In every case the fire judges the arrogant. Peter takes this inheritance and names its coming 'the day of God'.

The third strand is the thief and the new creation. Jesus said the Son of Man will come at an hour no one expects, Matthew 24:43 and 44 and Luke 12:39 and 40, and the image is repeated by Paul in 1 Thessalonians 5:2, and by John in Revelation 3:3 and 16:15. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth. Peter's hope in verse 13 is exactly this, and Revelation 21:1 shows it arriving. Psalm 90:4 and Habakkuk 2:3, quoted in Hebrews 10:37, give the patience of God and the certainty of the appointed time.

The passage is also treated as Scripture by Peter's own pen. In 3:15 and 16 he says Paul wrote about these matters, probably referring to passages like 1 Thessalonians 4 and 5 and Romans 2:4, and that the ignorant twist the letters 'as they do the rest of the Scriptures'. That makes this chapter a point where the apostolic writings are explicitly set beside the Old Testament.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Peter wants the church to hold two things at once that the scoffers say cannot go together, a Lord who has promised to return and a world that goes on. He does not deny that the days go by. He denies the conclusion drawn from it. The sceptics read delay as failure, and Peter reads it as mercy, and he supports the reading from God's own character and from the pattern of earlier history.

He also means the readers to answer not only the scoffers but themselves. The paragraph ends in a question about the kind of people believers ought to be, and the letter's closing words give the answer: be on guard, grow in grace and knowledge, 3:17 and 18. A hope that does not change a life is the hope of the scoffers in a different form. Peter writes so that a long wait will produce holiness, not boredom.

There is a pastoral gentleness in the warning. Peter calls his readers 'beloved' repeatedly, he reminds rather than rebukes, and he assumes that they know these things. His aim is to stir wholesome thinking, to wake a mind that has begun to doze in the long afternoon of waiting.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes the character of the last days, the scoffers' words, the course of the Day and the new heavens and earth. Those are statements of what will happen. The commands are few and clear: remember the words of prophets and apostles, do not let this one thing escape notice, live in holiness and godliness, look forward, be at peace and spotless, and be on guard.

It is easy to read verses 10 to 12 as a timetable or a technical description of physics. They are not. They are written in the language of the prophets, and Peter's reason for describing them is to ask what kind of people we ought to be, not to answer how the universe will end. Reading the verses to set dates, or to calculate when 'a day is like a thousand years', turns a call to holiness into a puzzle.

The statement that God is 'not wanting anyone to perish' describes His heart, and it is not a promise that every person will be saved. Verse 7 says the day brings 'destruction of ungodly men', and verse 9 is addressed to a church that is invited to repent. Both belong in the same chapter.

debates.question: What is the point of 'a day is like a thousand years', verse 8?

views.label: God is not bound by human time
views.case: Peter quotes Psalm 90:4 to say that God's sense of time is not ours. What feels like a long delay to us is a moment to Him, and so the lapse of years is no reason to doubt His promise. The line is an answer to the scoffers' appeal to the passing of the generations.

views.label: A rule for dating prophecy
views.case: Some early Christian writers took the verse as a key for mapping history into thousand-year days. Peter's context does not support this: the second half of the verse, 'a thousand years are like a day', cuts the other way, and there is no counting in the passage.

views.label: Both patience and nearness
views.case: A few point out that the two halves of the verse together say that God neither hurries nor drags. A long time is nothing to Him, and a short time is not too short to fulfil what He has said.

debates.bearing: The context turns the verse into a statement about God's character and not a calendar. The point is that years prove nothing, and the application is in verse 9, where patience takes the place of slowness.

debates.question: Whom does God not want to perish, verse 9?

views.label: God desires the salvation of every person
views.case: The verse says 'not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance', and Ezekiel 18:23 and 1 Timothy 2:4 speak in the same way. On this reading God's heart is open to all, and the delay gives time for all to be reached. Many Reformed writers, John Calvin among them, have affirmed that God is willing to receive all who come, while holding that He has chosen those He will bring.

views.label: The 'you' are the elect, and 'all' means all of them
views.case: Others point to the phrase 'with you' and say Peter writes to believers. On this reading God holds back until the last of His people have come to repentance, and 'anyone' and 'everyone' mean everyone of them. It stresses that the delay is for the sake of the elect.

views.label: Universal salvation
views.case: A small number argue that if God wants all to repent, all will. The text itself denies this, since verse 7 speaks of the destruction of ungodly men and verse 10 of a Day that comes as judgment.

debates.bearing: The immediate point is that the delay is mercy. Whichever way the verse is read, no one is excused, and the call to repentance is addressed to the readers and, through them, to the world.

debates.question: Will the present heavens and earth be destroyed or renewed, verses 10 to 13?

views.label: Annihilation and replacement
views.case: The language of 'disappear', 'destroyed' and 'melt' suggests that the present creation is done away with and a different one made. Revelation 20:11 says earth and heaven fled from the presence of the One on the throne, and Revelation 21:1 says the first heaven and earth passed away.

views.label: Purification and renewal
views.case: Others stress that the fire is a refining one and that the word for new, kainos, means new in quality, not a different thing made from nothing. Romans 8:19 to 21 speaks of the creation itself being set free from decay and brought into glory, and 1 Corinthians 3:13 says fire tests what is built, not that it destroys everything. The flood in verse 6 did not annihilate the earth but washed it, and the same pattern holds for fire.

views.label: Both, in different senses
views.case: Some hold that the present order of things, with its sin and decay, is destroyed, while the material creation is renewed. The elements dissolve, and the world as it is gives way to the world as it will be.

debates.bearing: The text says that the earth and its works will be laid bare or found, and that righteousness will be at home in what follows. The pastoral point does not turn on the answer: all that sin has made will go, and God's promise is of a world in which righteousness dwells.

debates.question: How do believers 'hasten' the Day, verse 12?

views.label: By holy living and prayer
views.case: The Greek verb can mean to hurry something along, and Peter links it to holiness and godliness. Believers speed the Day by repentance, by prayer, 'Your kingdom come', and by living as those who long for it.

views.label: By spreading the gospel
views.case: Since the delay exists so that people may repent, believers who bring the gospel to the world serve the purpose of the delay and so hasten its end, in line with Matthew 24:14.

views.label: By eagerly desiring it
views.case: The verb can also mean to be eager for something, with no suggestion that human action changes the time, which God alone knows, Mark 13:32. Peter's meaning is that believers should long for the Day.

debates.bearing: In every reading the effect is the same: believers are to live toward the Day, not away from it. Whether our part is in changing the time or only in desiring it, God alone appoints the hour.

study.originalLanguages:
The Greek of this chapter carries more argument than its English. In verse 1 the 'reminder' is hypomnesis, and 'wholesome' thinking is eilikrines dianoia, a mind that is sincere or unmixed, one that has been held up to the light and found without hidden stain. Peter's aim is to clear the mind of what has settled into it. In verse 2 he sets 'the commandment of the Lord and Savior' through the apostles beside the holy prophets, putting apostolic words on the same footing as the prophets.

Verse 5 says the scoffers 'deliberately overlook' the history. The Greek literally says that this escapes them 'as they wish', willing it so, and the verb 'escape notice' returns in verse 8 where Peter says 'do not let this one thing escape your notice'. The sceptics are choosing not to see, and the readers are told not to choose the same. The earth was 'formed' in verse 5 by a verb, synistemi, that Paul uses in Colossians 1:17 for Christ in whom all things 'hold together'. The creation is not self-sustaining; the word that made it holds it together.

In verse 7 the heavens and earth are 'reserved for fire', the verb is tereo, 'kept', as in 2:4, 9 and 17, and the participle that goes with it, thesaurizo, means stored up as in a treasury. The present world is kept, stored up for fire, as a person who hardens his heart 'stores up wrath' in Romans 2:5. The same word of God that makes the world also keeps it, for judgment.

Verse 9 says God is not 'slow'. The word and its idea come from Habakkuk 2:3, 'it will surely come and will not delay', quoted in Hebrews 10:37. The positive statement uses a verb for patience that Peter has already used in the opening of the sentence, and the clause 'not wanting' is boulomai, a word of settled purpose rather than passing wish. The goal is that all might 'come to repentance', and the verb chorein means to make room, to advance, to reach. Repentance is imagined as a place into which people may move, and God is holding the door.

Verse 10 has the most discussed text in the chapter. 'With a roar' is a word that imitates a rushing or whistling sound. The 'elements' are dissolved, from luo, to loose, a verb Peter repeats in verses 11 and 12, so that the picture is of the world coming undone. The end of the verse is a textual crux: some of the best early manuscripts read that the earth and its works 'will be found', heurethesetai, and later ones read 'will be burned up'. The BSB's 'laid bare' follows the first. The sense may be that everything is exposed before God, the same idea as 1 Corinthians 3:13, where the Day 'will bring it to light' and fire proves each person's work.

In verse 11 Peter asks what kind of people we ought to be, and the answer uses plural nouns, literally 'holy ways of life and acts of godliness'. Holiness is lived out in many practical forms, not in a single feeling. In verse 12 the verb 'hasten' is speudo, to hurry, used elsewhere of people moving quickly, as in Luke 2:16, and the verb for 'anticipate', prosdokao, is repeated in verses 12, 13 and 14. Three times in three verses Peter says the believers are waiting with expectancy, and each time it is linked to what they should be doing.

In verse 13 the righteousness 'dwells', from katoikeo, to settle and make one's home. Peter's first letter described believers as foreigners and exiles, 1 Peter 2:11, and here righteousness, which has been a wanderer in the old world, finally has a house.

typology.type: The flood and the fire, verses 5 to 7
typology.fulfillment: The world of Noah's day was flooded and perished, and Peter says that the present heavens and earth are kept for fire by the same word. The first judgment is both a warning and a pledge, because the flood really happened and so the fire will. Jesus uses the flood as the pattern for the day of the Son of Man, Matthew 24:37 to 39. The escalation is from a judgment that spared a remnant in an ark, Genesis 7:23, to the last judgment that comes with Christ, 2 Thessalonians 1:7 to 9, and it is followed by a creation not merely preserved but renewed. The type falls short because God promised after the flood never again to destroy all living creatures by water, Genesis 9:11, and said nothing of fire.

typology.type: The thief in the night, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: Jesus uses the householder who is robbed because he did not know the hour as a picture of readiness, Luke 12:39 and 40, and Paul tells the Thessalonians that the Day will come like a thief, 1 Thessalonians 5:2. The image gets its force from suddenness and from the loss of the unprepared. The escalation is that this thief takes nothing, but exposes everything, and the Lord who comes is the Master of the house and not an intruder. Revelation 16:15 shows the One who comes as a thief blessing the watchful. The picture falls short in that a thief is an enemy, while the One who comes is the Lord for whom the faithful are waiting.

typology.type: The new heavens and the new earth, verse 13
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 promise new heavens and a new earth that will endure, and Romans 8:19 to 21 says creation itself is waiting to be set free from decay. Peter says believers look forward to this because God promised. The correspondence is with the first creation, 'very good', Genesis 1:31, now restored after the curse. The escalation is that the new creation is not a return to Eden but a world where righteousness is at home and God dwells with man, Revelation 21:3. The type of Eden falls short in that it could be lost, while the new creation is secured by the One who makes all things new, Revelation 21:5.

typology.type: The delay and the long patience of God, verses 8 and 9
typology.fulfillment: Habakkuk is told that the vision awaits its time and will not delay, though it lingers, Habakkuk 2:3. Noah waited while the ark was built, and 1 Peter 3:20 says God waited patiently in his days. The long delay before the flood is a pattern for the long delay before the Day, in which God's patience gives time for repentance, as Romans 2:4 says His kindness leads to repentance. The escalation is that the final delay is bought by the cross, so that patience is not merely postponement but an offer made good. The pattern falls short because the time of Noah ended in judgment on those who had not come into the ark, while the present time is still open to all.

study.christ:
The whole chapter hangs on a person's return. The scoffers ask about 'the promise of His coming', and every verse of Peter's answer assumes that the One who is coming is Jesus, the 'Lord and Savior' of verse 2. The word 'Lord' in verses 8, 9 and 10 is naturally read as Him, since the Day of the Lord is the day on which Jesus comes. The One who is patient is the One who will judge, and His patience is the pause that He grants.

Christ is the reason the patience has a purpose. Verse 9 says God does not want anyone to perish, and the means by which anyone can be saved is the cross. Peter says in the next verses that the Lord's patience means salvation, 3:15, and the salvation he means is the one won in Christ, who bore the judgment that the Day will otherwise bring. The delay is not empty time; it is the time in which the gospel goes out, and the time exists because of what the Son has done.

The Day itself has Christ at its centre. Paul tells the Thessalonians that the Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven 'in blazing fire', 2 Thessalonians 1:7, and Jesus says that as the lightning flashes across the sky so will be the Son of Man in His day, Luke 17:24. The fire of Peter's chapter is the fire of His presence, and the new heavens and earth are the world He makes new, Revelation 21:5. Titus 2:13 calls the hope of believers 'the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ'. When Peter speaks of 'the day of God' in verse 12, the Day is God's through Christ.

There is also a pattern in the way Christ fulfils the promise. The thief language comes from His own lips, and the call to watchfulness is His. The scoffers' question, 'Where is the promise?', is answered by the One who said, 'Heaven and earth will pass away, but My words will never pass away', Matthew 24:35. The faithfulness of the promise rests on the faithfulness of the Promiser.

We should be careful with the details of the fire, since the passage does not say that the fire is Christ or that the elements stand for anything in Him. What Peter gives us is the plain connection: a Lord who has promised, who is patient because He saves, who will come as Judge, and who will make a home in which righteousness lives.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who speaks and whose word does things. By His word the heavens existed, by it the world was formed, by it the flood came and by it the present heavens and earth are kept for fire. Peter does not tell us that God has a plan, he tells us that God's word is the force behind all of history, so that a skeptic who says nothing changes has overlooked the thing that changes everything. The Lord who made the world is able to end it.

He is shown as patient. The patience is not a weakness, and the passage insists on this. God is 'not slow', which would imply that He is capable of lateness; He is patient, which means that He is able to act at once and chooses not to. Psalm 102:25 to 27 says that the heavens will wear out but that the LORD remains the same, and His years never end. A God who is not bound by time is the only kind who can be patient without anxiety.

He is also shown as one who wants. Verse 9 puts into words the desire of God that no one should perish. This is a window onto the heart of the God of the Bible, who says in Ezekiel 18:23 that He takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. The judgment of verse 10 is not the delight of a God who enjoys destruction. It is the last resort of a God who has been patient for as long as patience can serve.

He is holy and just. The fire is not a failure of control but the act of One who judges the world, and the righteousness that is to dwell in the new heavens and earth is His own character, which He will make the atmosphere of a whole creation. Hebrews 12:29 says 'our God is a consuming fire', and the end of the world is that fire come to rest on all that is not His.

The doctrine that holds all this together is that God is faithful. He keeps His promise, to judge and to renew, and the delay is part of the keeping. For worship the passage teaches us to hold a double attitude. We wait with reverence, for the Day is coming, and with gratitude, for the delay is an act of kindness which may be the reason any of us has been brought to repent. The people who can say 'we are looking forward' are the people who have learned to trust the patience of God.

crossReferences.note: A thousand years in God's sight are like a day that passes. Peter takes the line out of a psalm about human frailty and God's eternity, and uses it to answer the scoffers: time is not the measure of whether God keeps His word.

The vision awaits an appointed time and will surely come and not delay. The prophet had the same problem of waiting that Peter's readers had. Hebrews 10:37 quotes this text in the form 'He who is coming will come and will not delay', and Peter's 'not slow' belongs with it.

Jesus says no one knows the day or hour, compares the coming to the days of Noah, and says the Son of Man will come like a thief to a householder who was not watching. Peter's chapter is largely an expansion of these sayings, written by a man who had heard them.

Paul writes that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night while people say 'Peace and security', but that believers are not in darkness. Peter and Paul both use the thief to teach readiness and to say the Day will be a shock for the careless and no surprise to the alert.

Paul asks if anyone disregards the riches of God's kindness, tolerance and patience, not realizing that His kindness leads to repentance. It is the closest parallel to 2 Peter 3:9, and it shows how the delay and the call to repentance are linked in the apostolic teaching.

God asks whether He takes any pleasure in the death of the wicked, and says He would rather they turn from their ways and live. This is the Old Testament source of Peter's statement that God does not want anyone to perish, and it shows that the idea is not new.

God promises to create new heavens and a new earth, so wonderful that the former things will not be remembered. Peter's 'in keeping with God's promise' in verse 13 points to this text, and Isaiah 66:22 repeats it with the added note that it will endure.

John sees a new heaven and a new earth, the dwelling of God with man, and the end of death, mourning and pain. It is the vision of what Peter looks toward, and it shows the end of the story in which righteousness has made its home.

Paul says the creation waits in eager expectation, was subjected to futility in hope, and will be set free from decay into the glory of God's children. It shows that the physical world has a part in the hope, and it supports the reading that the fire cleanses rather than abolishes.

God shook the earth at Sinai and has promised to shake heaven too, so that the unshakable may remain, and the writer concludes that our God is a consuming fire. The text puts the removal of created things beside the gift of an unshakable kingdom, as Peter does.

The flood narrative begins with the LORD seeing that the wickedness of man was great and with Noah finding favor. It supplies the history that Peter says the scoffers have chosen to forget, and it shows that God does act in the world.

The great Day of the LORD is near, a day of wrath, and the whole earth will be consumed by the fire of His jealousy. Peter's picture of the Day draws on this prophetic stock, and the verses show that fire and judgment on the arrogant belong to the Old Testament's own language for the end.

study.oneStory:
The chapter stands at the end of the Bible's long argument about time. Genesis 1 and 2 give a world made by God's word and called good. Genesis 3 brings the curse, and from that moment the story is one of promise and waiting: the seed of the woman will come, the sons of Abraham will bless the nations, the Son of David will reign. Every generation after Eden has lived in the 'not yet', and the question 'How long?' runs through the Psalms, the Prophets and the cry of the martyrs in Revelation 6:10. Peter's scoffers say that the waiting proves the promise empty, and the whole of Scripture answers that the waiting is part of the promise.

The flood sits in the middle of the argument. It showed that God judges a world that has turned from Him and that He keeps a remnant, and it ended with a promise never to repeat it by water. Peter takes up the unfinished part, that a final judgment is still to come, and makes the flood the guarantee. The line from Noah through Abraham and Moses to the prophets is a line of warnings given and mostly not believed, and each fulfilled warning is a reason to trust the next.

The cross changes the meaning of the delay. Because the Son came and died and rose, the time between His first and second comings is an age of mercy in which the gospel goes to the nations. Paul says the creation groans like a woman in labor, Romans 8:22, and Peter says God is waiting for repentance. Both describe an age that is pregnant with what is to come.

The Day itself is the end of the fall. All that sin has built and all that the curse has marked will be undone, and the new heavens and earth will be the world as God meant it, with a home for righteousness. The prophets' fire is the fire that clears away what cannot stand. The hope of Isaiah 65 and 66 is realised in Revelation 21 and 22, where the tree of life returns, the curse is gone and God dwells with His people.

Peter's letter therefore ends where Scripture ends, with a call to live between the promise and its fulfilment. Believers are those who have received the promise and are waiting for its completion. The ones who scoff have forgotten where the world came from and where it is going; the ones who believe are told to grow, to be at peace and spotless in His sight, and to look forward to the world where everything that was lost in Genesis 3 is given back and more besides.

sermon.title: The Day of the Lord
sermon.why: From Begg's series A Study in 2 Peter, this message expounds 2 Peter 3:1-13 directly: the scoffers of the last days, the answer from God's word and the flood, the Lord's patience toward repentance, and the sudden Day of the Lord with the promise of the new creation. A clear, orthodox handling of this movement.

quiz.q: On what basis do the scoffers deny the promise of Christ's coming in verses 3 to 4?

options.text: They claim everything continues unchanged as it has from the beginning of creation.
options.note: Verse 4: their argument is from the apparent uniformity of the world since the fathers died.

options.text: They have carefully studied the prophets and found the promise false.
options.note: Peter says they deliberately overlook God's word and are driven by their own desires, not study.

options.text: They mock the promise while following their own evil desires.
options.note: True to verse 3, though the stated argument is the world's sameness in verse 4.

options.text: They believe Christ already returned in secret.
options.note: The scoffers deny His coming altogether; they do not claim a secret return.

quiz.q: How does Peter answer the charge that God is slow to keep His promise, verses 8 to 9?

options.text: The delay is God's patience, not wanting anyone to perish but all to come to repentance.
options.note: Verse 9: what looks like slowness is long-suffering mercy aimed at repentance.

options.text: God has simply forgotten the promise He made.
options.note: The opposite: no promise of God can fail, for He is not bound by time.

options.text: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, so He is not bound by our sense of time.
options.note: True to verse 8, though the heart of the answer is His patience toward repentance.

options.text: The promise applies to a later generation, not to Peter's readers.
options.note: Peter says the Lord is patient with you; the delay is mercy now, not a deferral to others.

quiz.q: What does Peter recall about God's word to refute the scoffers in verses 5 to 7?

options.text: By God's word the world was made and once destroyed by flood, and that same word now reserves it for fire.
options.note: Verses 5 to 7: God's word both created and judged the world, and holds it for the coming Day.

options.text: God's word promises the world will never change again.
options.note: The reverse: the world faces a decisive judgment by fire.

options.text: The present heavens and earth are reserved for the day of judgment.
options.note: True to verse 7, though Peter's fuller point spans creation, flood, and coming fire.

options.text: God's word applies only to the spiritual realm, not the physical world.
options.note: Peter's argument is precisely about the physical world made, flooded, and reserved for fire.

quiz.q: How does Peter describe the manner of the Day of the Lord's arrival in verse 10?

options.text: It will come suddenly and unexpectedly, like a thief.
options.note: Verse 10: the image of the thief presses watchfulness, echoing Jesus' own teaching.

options.text: It will be announced years in advance by clear signs everyone will heed.
options.note: The point is suddenness; it comes like a thief, catching the careless unprepared.

options.text: It will bring the dissolving of the heavens and the elements by fire.
options.note: True to verse 10, though the question asks about the suddenness of its arrival.

options.text: It will come only after the whole world has been converted.
options.note: Peter ties the Day to God's patience for repentance, not to universal conversion first.

quiz.q: In light of the coming Day, how should believers live, verses 11 to 13?

options.text: In holiness and godliness, looking forward to the new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells.
options.note: Verses 11 to 13: the certain end of the present order calls for holy, expectant living.

options.text: In fear and withdrawal, since nothing they do matters.
options.note: Peter calls for active holiness and hope, not fearful passivity.

options.text: By anticipating and hastening the coming of the day of God.
options.note: True to verse 12, though the fuller command includes holiness and the hope of the new creation.

options.text: By calculating the date of Christ's return from the signs.
options.note: The Day comes like a thief; the call is readiness, not date-setting.

questions: The scoffers argued that because life carries on unchanged, God will not act. Where are you tempted to read the world's ordinary sameness as evidence that God is distant or silent?
Peter reframes the delay of the Day as God's patience toward repentance. How does seeing the interval as mercy rather than absence change the way you pray for those who do not yet believe?
The Day will come like a thief. What would it look like for you to be genuinely ready today rather than assuming there is always more time?
Peter says the certainty of the coming Day should make us holy and godly. Which area of your life would most change if you truly lived as though this world is not the last word?
Believers look forward to a new heaven and new earth where righteousness dwells. How does that final hope steady you when the present world seems given over to injustice and decay?

translationNotes.note: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years echoes Psalm 90:4; the point is God's transcendence over time, not a formula for calculating the end.
Patient renders makrothymeo, long-suffering; not wanting anyone to perish expresses God's gracious disposition toward repentance.
The elements be destroyed renders a verb meaning dissolved, also in verses 11 and 12; a textual variant reads the earth will be laid bare, or found, while some manuscripts read burned up.
New in a new heaven and a new earth renders kainos, new in kind, a renewed and righteous creation, echoing Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for 2 Peter 3:1-13. All verses confirmed against the API.
